items.q: State Mitchell's definition of Machine Learning.
items.answer: *"A computer program is said to **learn** from experience **E** with respect to some class of tasks **T** and performance measure **P**, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E."* — a well-posed learning problem is the triple $\langle P, T, E\rangle$. **Example:** checkers — T = playing checkers, P = % games won, E = games played against itself.

items.q: For the EnjoySport dataset (Sky, Temp, Humidity, Wind, Water, Forecast → Enjoy): (i) How many concepts are possible? (ii) Explain the hypothesis ⟨Sunny, Warm, ?, Strong, Cool, Same⟩. (iii) Classify ⟨Sunny, Warm, High, ?, Cool, Change⟩.
items.answer:
**(i)** The instance space has $3\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2 = 96$ distinct instances (Sky has 3 values, the rest 2). The number of **possible concepts** = every labelling of those instances = $2^{96}$. *(The number of semantically distinct **conjunctive hypotheses** is $1 + 4\cdot3^5 = 973$.)*

**(ii)** ⟨Sunny, Warm, ?, Strong, Cool, Same⟩ accepts any instance that is Sky=Sunny **and** Temp=Warm **and** Wind=Strong **and** Water=Cool **and** Forecast=Same, with **Humidity = anything** ('?'). 

**(iii)** ⟨Sunny, Warm, High, ?, Cool, Change⟩ — '?' for Wind means any wind. It accepts instances that are Sunny ∧ Warm ∧ High ∧ Cool ∧ Change (any wind), i.e. classifies them **positive (Enjoy = Yes)**.

items.q: Define: (1) Most specific hypothesis, (2) Most general hypothesis, (3) Version space, (4) Occam's Razor, (5) Inductive bias.
items.answer: **(1) Most specific:** $\langle\emptyset,\dots,\emptyset\rangle$ — rejects every instance (accepts nothing). **(2) Most general:** $\langle?,\dots,?\rangle$ — accepts every instance. **(3) Version space** $VS_{H,D}$ = the set of **all hypotheses in H consistent with the training data D**. **(4) Occam's Razor:** prefer the **simplest** hypothesis that fits the data (shortest tree / fewest assumptions). **(5) Inductive bias:** the set of assumptions a learner uses to generalise to unseen instances; without it, no generalisation is possible (futility of bias-free learning).

items.q: Explain Entropy and Information Gain in the context of the ID3 algorithm.
items.answer:
**Entropy** measures impurity of a set $S$: $H(S) = -\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i$ (0 = pure, 1 = 50/50 for two classes). **Information Gain** of attribute $A$ = expected reduction in entropy from splitting on $A$:
$$\text{Gain}(S,A) = H(S) - \sum_{v\in\text{Values}(A)}\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)$$
ID3 **greedily chooses the attribute with the highest gain** at each node, recursing until each branch is pure (entropy 0 → leaf).

items.q: For a two-class problem with p₁ = p and p₂ = 1−p, write the equations for Entropy, Gini Index, and Misclassification error, and compute each for p = 0.4.
items.answer:
**Entropy** $H = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p) = -0.4\log_2 0.4 - 0.6\log_2 0.6 = \mathbf{0.971}$.

**Gini** $G = 1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2) = 1 - (0.16 + 0.36) = \mathbf{0.48}$.

**Misclassification error** $E = 1 - \max(p, 1-p) = 1 - 0.6 = \mathbf{0.4}$.

All three measure node impurity; entropy/Gini are smooth and used to drive splits, misclassification is less sensitive.

items.q: What is overfitting with respect to decision trees? Explain the techniques to overcome it.
items.answer:
**Overfitting:** the tree grows so specific to the training data (capturing noise) that it does **well on training but poorly on test** data. Formally, $h$ overfits if some $h'$ has higher training error but lower true-distribution error. **Fixes:**
- **Pre-pruning (early stopping):** stop growing when a split's gain falls below a threshold / max depth / min samples.
- **Post-pruning:** grow the full tree, then cut subtrees back to leaves if validation accuracy doesn't drop — **reduced-error pruning** (subtree → majority-class leaf) and **rule post-pruning** (convert to rules, drop weak preconditions). Post-pruning is generally more effective.
- Use a separate **validation set**; gather more/cleaner data.

| Pre-pruning | Post-pruning |
|---|---|
| Stop growing the tree **early** (before it fits perfectly) | Grow the **full** tree, then cut back |
| Halt when gain < threshold / depth / min samples reached | Replace subtrees with leaves if validation accuracy holds |
| Faster, but may stop too soon (a weak split might enable a strong one later) | Generally **more effective** (no need to guess when to stop) |

items.q: Predict whether there is a traffic jam for the query ⟨6,4,4,5⟩ (Fog, #Buses, #Cars, #Lorries) using K-NN with K=3 (Euclidean). Data: (10,10,12,1)Y, (1,2,6,3)N, (4,5,1,4)N, (8,3,7,3)Y, (2,5,4,2)N, (7,3,5,4)Y, (3,2,8,2)N, (9,3,5,4)Y.
Explain the Minkowski, Manhattan, and Euclidean distances.
items.answer:
For points $x, y$ with $d$ attributes:
- **Minkowski:** $\big(\sum_i |x_i-y_i|^q\big)^{1/q}$ — the general form.
- **Manhattan** ($q=1$): $\sum_i |x_i-y_i|$ — city-block / grid path.
- **Euclidean** ($q=2$): $\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-y_i)^2}$ — straight-line distance.
Manhattan and Euclidean are special cases of Minkowski. All require **feature scaling** so large-range attributes don't dominate.

items.q: A spam classifier's confusion matrix is: Actual Spam → (Pred Spam 120, Pred Normal 60); Actual Normal → (Pred Spam 40, Pred Normal 180). Find TP, TN, FP, FN, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity.
items.answer:
Taking Spam as positive: **TP=120, FN=60, FP=40, TN=180** (total 400).
- **Accuracy** $=\frac{TP+TN}{N}=\frac{300}{400}=\mathbf{0.75}$
- **Precision** $=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}=\frac{120}{160}=\mathbf{0.75}$
- **Recall** $=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}=\frac{120}{180}=\mathbf{0.667}$
- **Specificity** $=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}=\frac{180}{220}=\mathbf{0.818}$

items.q: A 2-class confusion matrix has Predicted-A row = (455, x1) and Predicted-B row = (82, x2). Given accuracy = 82% over 1200 samples, find x1 and x2.
items.answer:
Total: $455 + x_1 + 82 + x_2 = 1200 \Rightarrow x_1 + x_2 = 663$. Correct predictions (diagonal) = accuracy × total = $0.82\times1200 = 984$. The diagonal is $455 + x_2$ (A predicted A, B predicted B), so $455 + x_2 = 984 \Rightarrow \mathbf{x_2 = 529}$, and $x_1 = 663 - 529 = \mathbf{134}$.

**Check:** $455+134+82+529=1200$ ✓; accuracy $=(455+529)/1200=0.82$ ✓.

items.q: Briefly explain Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and the advantages of the ROC curve.
items.answer: **Accuracy** $=\frac{TP+TN}{N}$ (overall correctness). **Precision** $=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$ (of predicted-positives, how many are right). **Recall** $=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$ (of actual positives, how many caught). **F1** $=\frac{2PR}{P+R}$ (harmonic mean — punishes a low P or R). **ROC advantages:** plots TPR vs FPR across **all thresholds** → threshold-independent comparison; **AUC** summarises it in one number (1 = perfect, 0.5 = random); robust visual for comparing classifiers and choosing an operating point, even on **imbalanced** data.

items.q: Explain the procedure for estimating the parameters of Logistic Regression (gradient descent).
items.answer:
Model: $h_\theta(x)=\sigma(\theta^Tx)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\theta^Tx}}=P(y=1\mid x)$. Fit $\theta$ by **minimising the log-loss (cross-entropy)** cost (convex):
$$J(\theta)=-\tfrac1m\sum_i\big[y^{(i)}\log h_\theta(x^{(i)})+(1-y^{(i)})\log(1-h_\theta(x^{(i)}))\big]$$
**Gradient descent:** repeat (simultaneously for all $j$) $\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha\sum_i (h_\theta(x^{(i)})-y^{(i)})x_j^{(i)}$ until convergence. (Squared error is avoided — non-convex with the sigmoid.) Use feature scaling and a vectorised implementation; predict $\hat y=1$ if $h_\theta(x)\ge0.5$ (i.e. $\theta^Tx\ge0$).

items.q: Define Overfitting & Underfitting, Version Space, and the Bias–Variance Dilemma.
items.answer: **Overfitting:** model captures noise → low train error, high test error (low bias, **high variance**). **Underfitting:** model too simple to capture the pattern → high train & test error (**high bias**, low variance). **Version space:** set of all hypotheses consistent with the training data. **Bias–Variance dilemma:** total error $=\text{Bias}^2+\text{Variance}+\sigma^2$; as model complexity rises, bias falls but variance rises — you cannot minimise both at once, so you trade them off at the complexity that minimises total error.

items.q: For a built decision tree, how do you extract decision rules?
items.answer: Each **root-to-leaf path** becomes one **IF–THEN rule**: the conjunction (AND) of the attribute tests along the path forms the antecedent, and the leaf's class is the consequent. e.g. path Outlook=Sunny → Humidity=High → leaf 'No' gives **IF Outlook=Sunny ∧ Humidity=High THEN No**. The whole tree = the disjunction (OR) of all such rules. Rules can then be pruned independently (rule post-pruning).
